source.title: Managing Shoulder Instability in the Contact and Collision Athlete

paper.citation: Lau E.N., Brown C.L., Saggar R., Mullen J., Olawin A., Lunn K., et al. Managing Shoulder Instability in the Contact and Collision Athlete. Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine. 2026;19(1):34. doi:10.1007/s12178-026-10011-4.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How should anterior and posterior shoulder instability be assessed and managed in contact and collision athletes to restore stability, function, and safe sport participation? Participants: No new cohort; the review summarizes clinical studies of patients and athletes with shoulder instability. Sport and level: Contact and collision sports, with mechanisms and decisions applicable to rugby and American football. Design: Current narrative review. Exposure or intervention: Nonoperative rehabilitation and bracing; arthroscopic Bankart repair, remplissage, Latarjet, posterior capsulolabral repair, and other stabilization procedures.
paper.tldr: The review cites randomized trials reporting recurrent anterior instability near 10% after operative intervention versus 70% after nonoperative treatment in high-risk populations; these estimates come from underlying studies and are not a pooled effect calculated by this review. Arthroscopic Bankart repair recurrence rates were reported between 4% and 19%, with failure risk associated with multiple dislocations, hyperlaxity, glenoid bone loss, off-/near-track lesions, and longer delay to surgery. A contact athlete with instability needs prompt sports-medicine assessment that distinguishes direction, recurrence, apprehension, bone loss, track status, position demands, season timing, and future goals.
paper.methods: Design: Current narrative review. Exposure or intervention: Nonoperative rehabilitation and bracing; arthroscopic Bankart repair, remplissage, Latarjet, posterior capsulolabral repair, and other stabilization procedures. Comparator: Treatment and procedure comparisons reported in underlying trials, cohorts, and reviews. Measurements and outcomes: Recurrent instability, bone loss, complications, patient-reported outcomes, return to sport, residual deficits, and revision. Analysis: Narrative synthesis rather than new quantitative pooling.
paper.findings: The review cites randomized trials reporting recurrent anterior instability near 10% after operative intervention versus 70% after nonoperative treatment in high-risk populations; these estimates come from underlying studies and are not a pooled effect calculated by this review. Arthroscopic Bankart repair recurrence rates were reported between 4% and 19%, with failure risk associated with multiple dislocations, hyperlaxity, glenoid bone loss, off-/near-track lesions, and longer delay to surgery. For contact/collision athletes with on- or near-track lesions and subcritical bone loss, the reviewed evidence associated Bankart repair plus remplissage with recurrence as low as 5% and outcomes similar to Latarjet in selected cases. Latarjet recurrence was reported as low as 0.8% in recurrent instability with critical bone loss, but complication rates were reported as high as 30%. After arthroscopic Bankart repair, a cited cohort found residual strength or functional deficits in 38 of 43 athletes at six months, supporting criteria-based rather than time-only clearance.
paper.limitations: The review does not report systematic methods or formal certainty/risk-of-bias grading, so evidence selection and weighting may be subjective. Underlying estimates mix first-time and recurrent instability, anterior and posterior pathology, bone-loss severity, surgical techniques, sports, ages, and competitive levels. High same-season return after nonoperative care is not equivalent to low recurrence; the review emphasizes that many athletes experience another instability event. Procedure comparisons are vulnerable to treatment-selection confounding because anatomy and risk often determine the operation. Reported thresholds for “critical” glenoid bone loss vary, and procedure choice cannot be reduced to one percentage. Return at 4–6 months is a broad clinical timeline, not evidence that every athlete is functionally ready.
paper.practicalImplications: A contact athlete with instability needs prompt sports-medicine assessment that distinguishes direction, recurrence, apprehension, bone loss, track status, position demands, season timing, and future goals. In-season return decisions should explicitly discuss recurrent instability and progressive tissue/bone damage. After treatment, clearance should combine pain-free motion, strength, stability/apprehension, task-specific exposure, functional testing, and psychological readiness. Procedure and rehabilitation decisions belong to the treating surgical and rehabilitation team.
